newsitem.title: USA: NU urges prompt debt relief in Conn. dereg.
newsitem.headline: NU urges prompt debt relief in Conn. dereg.

text.p: Northeast Utilities warned Thursday that meeting Connecticut's targeted 10 percent cut in electricity rates by deregulating the state's power industry would be hard without accelerating securitization plans.

"The difficulty will be that if securitization is not an allowed means for us to achieve cost savings, it's going to be very, very difficult for us to achieve a 10 percent (rate) cost savings," Richard Soderman, director of regulatory planning at Northeast Utilities, told Reuters.
Soderman was attending a conference in Hamden, Conn. on the state's economic outlook in the next century, where he was a panelist on energy issues.
The proposed rate cut is a main feature of Connecticut's move to lower power prices, among the highest in the nation, by introducing open competition in its electricity industry.

Securitization involves issuing bonds to cover the debt, or stranded costs, taken on by utilities to build power plants and other infratructure in the days of strict regulation when such costs could be passed on to consumers.
Northeast Utilties, weighed down by heavy debt tied to its three idled Millstone nuclear power units in Waterford, Conn., estimates its stranded costs at about $3 billion.
"We think securitizaton is the best way to lower our costs, and if we can lower our costs, we can lower our rates," Soderman said, adding "we've committed to doing a five percent (rate cut) or more."
He said the company was ready to push forward with securitization, but that the state bill currently under consideration would not open that possiblity until 1999.
"We're troubled by that because we didn't want to wait that long. We think it can be done sooner. We thought that could be accomplished by year-end or early 1998," he said.
A revised draft of Connecticut's electricity deregulation bill is expected next week.
Soderman said that draft "will really frame the issues."
Connecticut's move toward deregulation is under some time pressure. The legislature's current session ends June 4, and they do not recovene until next year.
"I think there's a great intent to have something happen in this session, but how it turns out and how it affects us is just speculation," he said.
Northeast Utilities earlier proposed phasing in competition in the state's power industry over five years, starting in 1998 and reaching a fully deregulated market in 2003.
Northeast Utilities' Connecticut subsidiary, Connecticut Light & Power Co, with 6,000 employees and 1.1 million customers, is by far the state's biggest utility.
